title: Chapter 19: Testing Your Code: assert and pytest
video_title: Python Chapter 19: Testing Your Code, assert and pytest
summary: Asha's module checked itself with printed lines that nobody read. Follow her as she turns them into real tests: assert, a pytest file, reading a failure, edge cases, decimals and test-first thinking. Then watch her check an AI's tests by breaking her code on purpose, and catch tests that could never fail.

scenes.title: Why this matters
scenes.direction: Define a test, then why tests matter when people and AI change code.

visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: A **test** runs your code with a known input and checks the result against the answer you expect.
If the result is wrong, the test fails loudly.
Run the tests after every change, by you, a colleague or an AI.

segments.say: A test runs your code with a known input, and checks the result against the answer you expect. If the result is wrong, the test fails loudly.
Tests keep code working. Every time you, a colleague or an AI changes it, you run the tests again.

scenes.title: The idea: input, run, compare
scenes.direction: Teach the three parts with the diagram, then the three kinds of check, then the smoke alarm and where it stops working. Then a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: Every test has three parts
visual.label: The idea
body: A known input, a run of the code, and a comparison with the expected result.
visual.pre:
known input        run the code          compare
  boxes for 40  -->  boxes_needed(40)  -->  is it 4?
                                            yes: pass
                                            no:  FAIL

segments.say: Every test has three parts. A known input: 40 biscuits. A run of the code: boxes needed. And a comparison: is it 4? Yes means pass. No means fail.

visual.heading: Three ways to check a result
visual.label: The idea
rows: Runs every test, then names each failure.

segments.say: There are three ways to check a result. A printed check prints False, and carries on.
An assert stops the program with an error.
And a pytest test runs every test, then names each one that failed.

visual.heading: A test is like a smoke alarm
visual.label: Analogy
items: It stays quiet while everything is fine.
It makes a loud noise the moment something goes wrong.
Where it stops working: a test checks only the inputs you wrote.

segments.say: Think of a test as a smoke alarm in the cafe kitchen. It stays quiet while everything is fine.
And it makes a loud noise the moment something goes wrong.
The comparison stops working at one point. An alarm watches the whole room. A test checks only the inputs you wrote.

visual.question: Which check stops the program when the result is wrong?
visual.explain: `assert` raises an `AssertionError` and stops the program.

segments.say: Quick check. Which of these stops the program when the result is wrong?

after.say: C. Assert. A printed check only prints False, and a comment does nothing at all.

items: A test: known input, run, compare.
A printed check is easy to miss.
A test checks only the inputs you wrote.

segments.say: Take a breather. Next, Asha sees why a printed check is not enough.

scenes.title: Steps 1 and 2: From print to assert
scenes.direction: Show the quiet False, ask what lines 5 and 6 print. Teach assert, show it passing, then failing with a message, and ask whether the report is saved.

visual.heading: Step 1: A printed check
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 1. Someone typed 1.01 as the tax rate, instead of 1.1. Look at line 2.
Line 5 checks the tea price with print. Line 6 saves the report.

after.say: False, then Report saved. The check found the problem, but the program saved the report anyway.

visual.heading: Step 2: assert, when the check is true

segments.say: Step 2. An assertion is a statement that a condition must be true. You write assert, then the condition.
Here the tax rate is right. Both conditions are true, so assert does nothing, and line 7 saves the report.

visual.heading: Step 2: assert, when the check is false
visual.hidden_text: Predict what happens before it appears.

segments.say: Now the wrong rate again, on line 2.
When an assert condition is false, Python stops with an Assertion Error. After a comma, you can add a message. Line 6 would save the report.

after.say: No. Line 5 stops the program, so the report is never saved.
And the message says exactly what was wrong: tea with tax should be 3.85.

scenes.title: Step 3: Your first pytest file
scenes.direction: Install and run commands in a table, then the module, then the test file with its naming rules, ask how many tests and whether they pass. Then a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: Step 3: Install and run pytest
visual.label: Build it

segments.say: Step 3. pytest is a popular testing tool. It does not come with Python, so you install it once with pip, Python's package installer.
On macOS and Linux, type python3 instead of python. You will learn more about packages in Chapter 24.
Then you run a test file like this. The dash q option asks for a short, quiet report.

visual.heading: Asha's module, with one new tool

segments.say: Here is Asha's module from Chapter 18: with tax, and money.
She adds boxes needed, from the AI section of Chapter 18. Line 18 rounds up with math dot ceil. Run on its own, the module prints nothing.

visual.heading: A test file for pytest
visual.hidden_text: Predict the report before it appears.

segments.say: A test file has two naming rules. The file name starts with test and an underscore. And every test is a function whose name starts the same way.
Line 2 imports the three tools. Each test has one assert, with an exact expected value.

ask.question: How many tests will pytest run, and will they pass?

after.say: Three tests, and all three pass. Each dot is one passing test.
The last line counts them, and shows how long the run took. That time changes on every run.

visual.question: Which function will `pytest` run as a test?
visual.explain: pytest runs functions whose names start with `test_`.

segments.say: Quick check. Which of these functions will pytest run?

after.say: D. Test tea. Its name starts with test and an underscore. Tea test ends with it, so pytest skips it.

items: `assert` stops the program when a check is false.
Test files and test functions start with `test_`.
Each dot is one passing test.

segments.say: Breather. Next, Asha breaks her module on purpose, to see what a failure looks like.

scenes.title: Step 4: Read a failure
scenes.direction: Show the broken copy's line 18, ask which test fails, then read the report from the top.

visual.heading: Step 4: A broken copy, on purpose

segments.say: Step 4. Asha copies her files into a folder called broken. In the copy, line 18 uses round instead of math dot ceil. That is the AI's mistake from Chapter 18.

visual.heading: The same three tests, on the broken copy
visual.hidden_text: Predict the report before it appears.

segments.say: She runs the same three tests on the broken copy. Remember: round goes to the nearest whole number.

ask.question: Which of the three tests will fail?

after.say: The third one. The first line shows two dots and an F. F means one test failed.
The report names the test, and its line: 14.
The line that starts with E shows the values. Boxes needed returned 3, but the test expected 4. The last line counts one failed and two passed.

scenes.title: Steps 5 and 6: Edge cases and decimals
scenes.direction: Teach edge cases, ask which one catches round, then decimals: ask which test fails, then round and approx.

visual.heading: Step 5: Test the edge cases

segments.say: Step 5. An edge case is an unusual input at the limit of what a function must handle.
For boxes, the edges are no biscuits, exactly one full box, and one biscuit more than a box. On the working module, all three pass.

visual.heading: The edge cases, on the broken copy
visual.hidden_text: Predict the report before it appears.

segments.say: Now Asha runs the edge cases on the broken copy. Remember: round goes to the nearest whole number.

ask.question: On the broken copy, which edge case fails: 0, 12 or 13?

after.say: 13. 13 divided by 12 is about 1.08, and round turns that into 1 box. The test expected 2. The other two still pass.
So good tests check normal values and edge values. Each catches mistakes from a different side.

visual.heading: Step 6: Test decimal results safely
visual.hidden_text: Predict the report before it appears.

segments.say: Step 6. In Chapter 2 you saw that point 1, three times, is not exactly point 3. Here are three tests of that total.
Line 12 rounds the total to two decimal places. Line 17 uses pytest dot approx, which accepts a value that is very close.

ask.question: Which of the three tests fails?

after.say: The first one, test exact. The total is 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3.
The other two pass. For decimals, round both sides, or use approx.

scenes.title: Step 7: Write the test first
scenes.direction: The USD rule. Ask whether the new test passes on the current module, read the diff, then the change. Quiz and breather.

visual.heading: Step 7: The test comes first
visual.hidden_text: Predict the report before it appears.

segments.say: Step 7. The cafe owner wants every price label to start with U S D. Before Asha changes money, she writes the test for the new rule.

ask.question: Will this test pass on Asha's current module?

after.say: No, and that is what she expects. The money function still returns 4.00.
The minus line shows what the test expected. The plus line shows what the function returned.

visual.heading: Then she changes the code

segments.say: Now she changes line 13, and runs the test again. It passes. This is test first thinking: a test that fails before the change and passes after it proves the change did its job.

visual.question: You write a test for a new rule before you change the code. What should happen when you first run it?
visual.explain: The code does not follow the new rule yet, so the test fails. After the change, it passes.

segments.say: Quick check. You write a test for a new rule, before you change the code. What should happen the first time you run it?

after.say: B. It fails. The code does not follow the new rule yet. After the change, it passes.

items: Edge cases: zero, an exact limit, one more.
Compare decimals with `round()` or `approx`.
Test first: fail, change, pass.

segments.say: Breather. Now Asha puts everything together, in one test file.

scenes.title: See the outcome: the test file
scenes.direction: Return to the mission file, walk the tests, ask how many dots, reveal, then hand over to the AI feature.

visual.heading: Mission complete: Asha's test file
visual.hidden_text: Predict the report before it appears.

segments.say: Back to the mission. Lines 5 and 9 test the tax. Line 11 rounds the decimal total first.
Line 15 tests the new U S D label. Lines 18 to 26 test the boxes: normal values, and then the edges. A test can hold several asserts.

ask.question: How many dots will pytest print?

after.say: Five dots, one for each test function, and five passed. A test with three asserts still counts as one test.
Now, after every change, Asha runs one command. Mission complete!
Next, Asha asks an AI assistant to write tests too, one stage at a time.

scenes.title: Work with AI: six stages, one test file
scenes.direction: Teach the skill. One conversation per stage, all about a test file for cafe_tools. Generate: tests that cannot fail. Test: the broken copy. Debug: an exact decimal. Improve: the AI deletes two useful tests.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: check the tests
visual.label: Before you start
items: A test that can never fail looks exactly like a test that passes.
Break a copy of the code on purpose. Good tests fail on it.
Never paste private data. You are responsible for the tests you keep.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill: check that the AI's tests really test something. A test that can never fail looks exactly like a test that passes.
So break a copy of the code on purpose. Good tests fail on it. And never paste private data.

visual.heading: Plan: inputs and expected results

messages.text: I am learning pytest. My function boxes_needed rounds up to boxes of 12. Do not write code yet. List the inputs I should test, with the exact expected result for each.

1. 40 biscuits: 4 boxes, a part box.
2. 24 biscuits: 2 boxes, an exact division.
3. 0 biscuits: 0 boxes.
4. 12 and 13 biscuits: 1 and 2 boxes, the edge of one box.
I checked each one by hand: 40 divided by 12 is 3.33, so 4 boxes. They are all right.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha asks for the inputs to test, each with its exact expected result. No code yet.
The AI lists a part box, an exact division, zero, and the edge of one box.
Asha works out every expected result herself, by hand.

visual.heading: Write: her own tests first

messages.text: First I wrote two tests myself. Do not change them. Which behaviour do they not test yet?
They test an exact division and a part box. They do not test 0 biscuits, or the edge between 12 and 13.

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha writes two tests herself: 24 biscuits, and 40 biscuits. She asks the AI what they do not test yet.
The AI names zero, and the edge between 12 and 13. She will check the AI's file for those too.

visual.heading: Generate: a test file from the AI

messages.text: Write pytest tests for my cafe_tools module. They must catch any mistake in boxes_needed.
Here are three tests. They will catch any mistake in `boxes_needed`.

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Asha asks the AI for a test file that catches any mistake in boxes needed.
The AI writes three tests, and makes a big promise.

visual.heading: The AI's tests: all three pass

segments.say: On Asha's working module, all three pass. Look at the two box tests. Line 10 uses 24 biscuits. And the test on line 14 calls boxes needed with zero.

ask.question: The AI says these tests catch any mistake in `boxes_needed`. Is it right?

after.say: No. 24 divides exactly, so even round gives 2. And line 15 has no assert, so that test can never fail.

visual.heading: Test: run them on the broken copy

messages.text: My broken copy uses round instead of math.ceil. Which of your three tests should fail on it, and why?
None of them. 24 divided by 12 is exactly 2, so round gives the right answer. And test_zero has no assert, so it can never fail.

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha asks which of the AI's tests should fail on her broken copy.
This time the AI admits it: none of them.

visual.heading: On the broken copy: the AI's tests

segments.say: She runs them on the broken copy anyway. Three passed. The tests did not see the broken code.

visual.heading: On the broken copy: Asha's own tests

segments.say: Then she runs her own two tests on the same copy. The test for 40 biscuits fails, as a good test should.

visual.heading: The AI's seven tests, on the working module

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. The AI writes a better file, with seven tests. But on Asha's working module, one test fails: test two items, on line 11.

visual.heading: Debug: is the code or the test wrong?

messages.text: Your new test file fails on my working module. Here is the failing test, and the report says: assert 3.3000000000000003 == 3.3. Is the code or the test wrong? Explain why first.
The test is wrong, not the code. 1.1 plus 2.2 is stored as 3.3000000000000003. Round the total to 2 decimal places before you compare.

segments.say: She pastes the failing test and the values from the report.
She asks whether the code or the test is wrong. The AI reads the values: the test compares decimals exactly. Round the total first.

visual.heading: The fixed file, on the working module

segments.say: With the total rounded on line 11, all seven tests pass on the working module.

visual.heading: The fixed file, on the broken copy

segments.say: And on the broken copy, two tests fail: 40 biscuits and 13 biscuits. Now the tests can see the broken code.

visual.heading: Improve: before you delete a test

messages.text: All seven tests pass. Suggest at most one improvement, with one reason.
Delete test_full_boxes and test_zero. The tests for 40 and 13 already check rounding up, so those two repeat them.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Asha asks for one improvement.
The AI says: delete the tests for 24 and for zero, because 40 and 13 already check rounding up.

visual.heading: Another broken copy: Asha's old bug

segments.say: Asha remembers her own bug from Chapter 18: double slash, then plus 1. It was wrong for 24 biscuits. She makes a second broken copy with that bug.

visual.heading: The shorter file, on Asha's old bug

segments.say: The shorter file passes on it. Five passed. Without those two tests, her old bug would slip through.

visual.heading: The full file, on Asha's old bug

segments.say: The full file catches it: 24 biscuits gives 3, and zero biscuits gives 1. So Asha keeps every test. The AI was wrong again.

visual.question: All of an AI's tests pass. What is the best next check?
options: Run them on a copy you broke on purpose
Ask the AI if the tests are good
Delete the tests that look alike
Add print lines to the tests
visual.explain: Good tests fail on broken code. If nothing fails, the tests are too weak.

segments.say: Quick check. All of an AI's tests pass. What is the best next check?

after.say: A. Run them on a copy you broke on purpose. Good tests fail on broken code.

items: Plan, write, generate, test, debug, improve.
A test with no assert can never fail.
Before you delete a test, check what it catches.

segments.say: Breather. You watched Asha check every AI test, and catch two weak suggestions by breaking the code on purpose.
Next, the mistakes beginners make with tests.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistake 1 is a spot-it on the naming rule. Mistakes 2 and 3 call back. Mistake 4 is a spot-it on the import.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the report appears.

segments.say: Mistake 1. Asha runs this file with pytest. Remember the naming rule from step 3.

ask.question: pytest says that no tests ran. Why?

after.say: The function name does not start with test and an underscore, so pytest skips it. Rename it test tea tax.
after.heading: Mistake 1: a test without the test_ prefix

visual.heading: Mistakes 2 and 3: you have seen them
visual.label: Common mistakes
items: A test with no `assert` always passes. Every test needs an `assert` with an exact expected value.
Comparing decimals exactly can fail on correct code. Use `round()` or `pytest.approx()`.

segments.say: Mistake 2 was in the AI's first file: a test with no assert. It always passes.
Mistake 3 was in its second file: an exact comparison of decimals. Round both sides, or use approx.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: spot this one too
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the report appears.

segments.say: Mistake 4. Look at the import on line 2, and the test on line 6.

after.say: Boxes needed is never imported, so the test stops with a Name Error. Add it to line 2.
after.heading: Mistake 4: a missing import

after.say: A Name Error inside a test means the test itself is wrong, not the code it tests.

scenes.title: Recap
scenes.direction: Each recap point appears as it is spoken, then the badge.

visual.heading: Recap
visual.label: What you learned
items: A test runs code with a known input and compares the result with the expected answer.
`assert condition, "message"` stops the program when the condition is false.
`pytest` runs every `test_` function and reports each failure by name, line and value.
Test normal values and edge cases. Compare decimals with `round()` or `pytest.approx()`.
Write the test first: it fails before the change and passes after it.
Break a copy of the code on purpose: good tests fail on broken code.

segments.say: Let's recap. A test runs code with a known input, and compares the result with the answer you expect.
Assert stops the program when its condition is false.
pytest runs every test function, and names each failure, its line and its values.
Test normal values and edge cases, and compare decimals with round or approx.
Write the test first. And break a copy of the code on purpose: good tests fail on it.
Mission complete! You earned 100 XP and the Quality Guard badge.
